utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Are the interpreters ready? The visitors in the public gallery can hear the proceedings as well? The registrar; fellow Judges? Fine. The Trial Chamber I was the following Judges: Presiding Judge Claude Jorda; Mrs. Elizabeth Odio-Benito; and Judge Fouad Riad in the case of the Prosecutor against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. This is a review of the indictment under Rule 61. Now, in their Decisions rent rendered respectively on 25 July and 16 November 1995, Judges Claude Jorda Fouad Riad confirm the indictments issued by the Prosecutor against Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic. On the same dates, they issued warrants of arrest with orders for surrender against the two accused. Now, these warrants were sent to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Bosnian Serb administration at Pale, and so far they have not been executed. The Confirming Judges, in their decisions of 18 June 1996, considered that a reasonable time had elapsed since the warrants of arrest were issued and therefore invited the Prosecutor to report on the measures taken to effect personal service of the indictments or to inform the accused of their existence. Satisfied by the steps the Prosecutor had taken, in those same decisions the Judges ordered that he submit both indictments to the Trial Chamber for joint review during a public hearing, pursuant to the provisions of Rule 61 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence ("the Rules"). During its review, the Trial Chamber must consider whether there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused committed one or all of the offences for which they are charged in the indictment. To that end, it has reviewed all the evidence submitted to the Confirming Judges, as well as the additional material produced during the hearing. It also heard the witnesses who had been called and interviewed by the Prosecutor and two amici curiae, Mrs. Rehn, Special Rapporteur for the United Nations Commission on Human Rights, and Mrs. Cleiren, who is a member of the Commission of Experts established pursuant to Resolution 780 of the Council of Security, and the Chamber had to review the legal classification of the acts by the Prosecutor so that it could verify that its jurisdiction had been established at this stage. Now, recourse to the Rule 61 proceedings permits International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, which is not have its own police force, to react to the failure of the accused to appear voluntarily and to the failure to execute the warrants issued against them. Should the reviewing Trial Chamber review the indictments, it must issue international warrants of arrest. It may also note that the failure to execute the initial warrants of arrest may be acquired to the failure or refusal to cooperate by the State or States to which they were transmitted, and it may request the President of the Tribunal to inform the Security Council of that failure. The Rule 61 proceedings permit the charges in the indictment and the supporting material to be publicly and solemnly exposed. When called to appear by the Prosecutor, the victims may use this forum to have their voices heard and to become a part of history. The organs of international criminal justice, which cannot accommodate the failures of individuals or states, must pursue the mission of revealing the truth about the acts perpetrated and the suffering endured, as well as identifying and arresting those accused of responsibility. Prior to the Rule 61 hearings on 27 June and 5 July, and after having heard their oral submissions, the Trial Chamber reviewed two applications from the attorneys assigned by Radovan Karadzic. They were Mr. Pantelic from Belgrade, as well as Messrs. Medvene and Ranley from the California bar. And they were to represent him before the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, and they had requested access to all the documents and relevant files which the Prosecutor would submit during the proceedings. In decisions rendered on those two dates, the Trial Chamber, noting the powers of attorney lodged on behalf of Radovan Karadzic, invited the registrar to read the two indictments issued against the accused in the presence of the first attorney chosen. Rejecting the requests filed by the attorneys, it granted them observer status but required them to observe the proceedings from the public gallery. Now, we're going to begin by describing the indictments and then we're going to go on with a joint review thereof. The Chamber was seized of the review of two indictments. The former, confirmed on 25 July 1995, states that Radovan Karadzic, President of the Bosnian Serb administration, and Ratko Mladic, Commander of the Bosnian Serb army, are responsible for a series of serious violations of international humanitarian law allegedly committed by the forces of the Bosnian Serb Administration in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina since May 1992. Now, the indictment contains 16 counts set out in they parts. The Chamber notes that all of them pertain to offences within the Tribunal's jurisdiction, namely, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, violations of the laws or customs of war, genocide, and crimes against humanity. Now, the charges of crimes against humanity refer to persecution on political, racial and religious grounds of Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat civilians, as well as to the sniping campaign against the civilian population of Sarajevo. These same acts or also separately indicted in other counts of the indictment. The charge of genocide is invoked for the internment of civilians in detention facilities and inhumane treatment therein. Characterised as grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 are: the unlawful confinement of civilians in camps, the extensive destruction of property, and the appropriation and plunder of property. Characterised as violations of the laws or customs of war are: the unlawful confinement of civilians, the shelling of such gatherings, the destruction of sacred sites, the appropriation and plunder of property, and the sniping at civilians in Sarajevo. For taking United Nations peacekeepers hostage and using them as human shields, the accused are considered to be responsible for grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and violations of the laws and customs of war. Now, the second indictment, confirmed on 16 November 1995, relates to serious violations of international humanitarian law allegedly committed by the forces of the Bosnian Serb Administration during the takeover of the Srebrenica safe area in the east of Bosnia and Herzegovina in July 1995. Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic are charged with genocide, crimes against humanities, and violations of the laws and customs of war for the summary execution of Bosnian Muslims at and around Potocari and Karakaj, as well as in the woods in the direction of Tuzla. The Chamber notes that boat of the indictments which are before it involve the same individuals, Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, and that both invoke the individual criminal responsibility of the accused on account of their positions of authorities in the Bosnian Serb Administration. For these reasons, the Chamber considered it appropriate to join the two indictments for further review under Rule 61. So the Chamber's going to begin by describing the offences alleged in the indictments and the supporting evidence. It will then turn its attention to the alleged individual criminal responsibility of Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, first putting those acts in their historical, political, and military context, in particular, in late of the concept of ethnic cleansing, and then demonstrating the role of the two accused within an organisation. It will then legally characterise the acts in accordance with the Statute. Now, such a repetition of similar acts who were all aimed at the same kind of people and demonstrate the same desire to alienate the culture and religious rights give rise to the question as to the level of responsibility to which one has to go up to determine the conception, the planning, and organisation and then the execution of such an approach. Now, this consideration of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia can but lead to the conclusion that one has to consider a political responsibility at the highest level, the individual criminal responsibility of superiors, and in this case, those of political and military leaders. There is no historical example, taking into account the judgements handed down in Nuremberg and Tokyo, where it was not through an analysis of the conflict, considering the intent and the planning alongside the execution, that one could consider this kind of issue appropriately. Now, as said, we are going to begin with the offences charged. Now, what follows are allegations made in the supporting material submitted by the Prosecutor and in testimony heard during the proceedings. We're going to begin by considering the first indictment and move on to the second indictment. With regard to the first indictment, the charges against the accused in the first indictment relate to a series of acts which occurred between April 1992 and July 1995 in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They included setting up internment camps, targeting Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat political, intellectual, and professional leaders, shelling civilian gatherings, appropriating, plundering and/or destroying property and systematically destroying places of worship. The criminal acts charged will be examined in three main section main parts: crimes related to Bosnian Serb military operations, crimes related to the siege of Sarajevo, and crimes against United Nations personnel. One, crimes related to Bosnian Serb military operations. Now, these crimes may be further divided into four categories, (a) Unlawful confinement and related crimes. During the period in question, a network of camps which were managed and organised by civilian and military personnel and Bosnian Serb police, and which were located across the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina under Bosnian Serb occupation (Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje, Luka, Manjaca, Susica; KP Dom, Livade, Batkovic, et cetera) was used to intern thousands of civilian Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, including women, children, and elderly people who had been systematically selected and assembled for national, ethnical, political, or religious reasons. Detained for weeks, months, or even years under inhuman living conditions involving inadequate rations and lack of medical care and proper hygiene, the civilians were then either executed, subjected to mistreatment and other physical and mental harm calculated to bring about their physical destruction, or used as human shields against other troops. After their execution, the remains of the victims from the KP Dom and Luka camps were allegedly thrown into the nearby Drina and Sava Rivers. In the Omarska camp, many detainees were said to have been burned alive by soldiers celebrating St. Peter's Day, a Serbian family saint's day, in July 1993. Inside the camps or at other places, many of the women and girls being detained were allegedly systematically raped and/or subjected to other forms of sexual assault by Serbian soldiers and police or by their agents with the consent and the complicity of the officials of the detention units. Some of the camps were nothing less than specialised centres for the rape of women. On a smaller scale, many men were also victims of rape and sexual assault by the Serbian forces. On several occasions, brothers or parents were forced to have sexual contact with one another. Forms of sexual assault particularly degrading for women, and using a variety of objects, and the castration of men, sometimes performed under duress by prisoners on one another, was practised. Appropriation or plunder of property, destruction of places of worship. In the cities and villages of Bosnia and Herzegovina which had come under their command, the Bosnian Serb military personnel and police, along with other agents of the Bosnian Serb administration, committed arbitrary large-scale appropriation of real and movable property belonging to Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat civilians. Prior to the forced transfer, many detainees in the internment camps were forced to sign official Bosnian Serb documents by which they "voluntarily" gave up their titles of ownership and their possessions to the Bosnian Serb administration. With the approval and consent of the leaders of the internment camps, or on their instructions, many detainees were escorted out of the camps to their homes, industrial or commercial establishments, were forced to and own their funds and other valuables. Elsewhere, in order to rule out any possibility of return by the dispossessed, Bosnian Serb forces systematically destroyed buildings. The destruction took place both in areas where the hostilities had ceased and in which the populations had surrendered without resistance. In cities such as Foca, where Serbian and non-Serbian neighbourhoods were next to one another, Serbian neighbourhoods were carefully spared. Throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina under their control, Bosnian Serb forces also destroyed, quasi-systematically, the Muslim and Catholic cultural heritage, in particular, sacred sites. According to estimates provided at the hearing by an expert witness, Dr. Kaiser, a total of 1.123 mosques, 504 Catholic churches and five synagogues were destroyed or damaged, for the most part, in the absence of military activity or after the cessation thereof. This was the case in the destruction of the entire Islamic and Catholic heritage in the Banja Luka area, which had a Serbian majority and the nearest area of combat to which was several dozen kilometres away. All of the mosques and Catholic churches were destroyed. Some mosques were destroyed with explosives and the ruins were then levelled and the rubble thrown in the public dumps in order to eliminate any vestige of Muslim presence. Aside from churches and mosques, other religious and cultural symbols like cemeteries and monasteries were targets of the attacks. Expulsion and deportation: Thousands of civilians were unlawfully expelled or deported to other places inside and outside the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Removed from their homes, many civilians, including women, children, and elderly persons, were used in prisoner exchanges. The result of these expulsions was a partial or total elimination of Muslim and Bosnian Croats in some of Bosnian Serb-held regions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the municipality of Prijedor, Foca, Vlasenica, Brcko, and Bosanski Samac, to name but a few, the once non-Serbian majority was systematically exterminated or expelled by force or intimidation. Among the methods used to apply pressure, the Prosecutor noted a radio announcement which told Muslims to leave town or face execution and stated that "for a Serb killed at the front, ten Muslims were to be executed." At the same time, Bosnian Serb military and police personnel persecuted leaders and members of the non-Serbian political parties, especially the mainly Muslim Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, and the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, the main Croatian political party, in the towns of Prijedor, Vlasenica, Bosanski Samac, Brcko, and Foca. Based on the lists drawn by the SDS, the leaders were arrested, interned, subjected to physical abuse, and in many cases, executed. Generally speaking, Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat political, intellectual, and professional leaders were victims of persecution by Bosnian Serb groups. Shelling of civilian gatherings. Throughout the conflict, the strategy of Bosnian Serb forces consisted in indiscriminately targeting civilians. Such was the case during the entire siege of Sarajevo, and at times in the safe areas of Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, Bihac, and Tuzla. From July 1992 to July 1995, many civilian gatherings, particularly at stadiums or in public squares, were subject to shelling by Bosnian Serb military forces whose objective was to kill, terrorise, and demoralise the civilian population. Crimes related to the siege of Sarajevo: From 5 April 1992 to 31 May 1995, the city of Sarajevo was besieged by Bosnian Serb forces. During this period, the city was subjected to systematic and deliberate sniping campaign, the outbreak of which allegedly occurred on 6 April 1992 from the headquarters of the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, at the Holiday Inn. The snipers, who were members of the Bosnian Serb army, used very sophisticated weapons to shoot people while they were going about their daily business. Casualties included women, children, and the elderly. Crimes committed against United Nations military personnel: In response to the airstrikes of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) on Serbian military targets, between 26 May and 2 June 1995, Bosnian Serb forces took hostage some 284 United Nations peacekeepers assigned, inter alia, to the regions of the Pale, Sarajevo, and Gorazde. Around 26 May 1995, Bosnian Serb forces selected United Nations military observers in the Pale region and used them as "human shields." Those observers were tied to potential targets of NATO airstrikes, specifically the munitions depot at Joharinski Potok, the radar facility site at Jahorina, and the nearby communications centre. High-level Bosnian Serb political and military delegations, which included, inter alia, Professor Koljevic, the then Vice-president Republika Srpska and President of the State Committee for Cooperation with the United Nations and other humanitarian organisations, even inspected and photographed the scene. According to one of the hostages, Captain Rechner, a Canadian military observer who was stationed in Pale and was in charge of, among other things, liaison between the United Nations Protection Force (UNPROFOR) and Bosnian Serb Administration, and who was often in contact with Radovan Karadzic's cabinet, the hostage-taking had been officially decided at the highest level of the chain of command. Now we will look at the charges in the second indictment. The charges against Karadzic and Mladic in the second indictment relate to a series of crimes allegedly committed during the military operations which preceded and followed the fall of Srebrenica enclave in July 1995. Due to the military occupation of their villages in Eastern Bosnia by the Bosnian Serb forces, the Muslim people of this region fled, in particular towards the enclaves of Gorazde, Zepa, Tuzla, and Srebrenica. In order to provide them with the requisite protection, the Security Council of the United Nations, acting pursuant to Chapter VII of the Charter, demanded in its Resolution 819 of 16 April 1993, that the parties to the conflict regard the Srebrenica enclave as a safe area and as such not subject it to armed attack or any other hostile act. Besieged since April 1993, the Srebrenica enclave was targeted, from 6 July 1995, by the shelling of Bosnian Serb forces to whom it fell on 11 July 1995. This was followed by an exodus of 40.000 Muslims who had lived in the safe area. Initially, the populations of the enclave gathered in and around the United Nations Srebrenica compound. Then, victimised by shelling from Bosnian Serb forces, they adopted two different lines of conduct. Several thousand women, children, and mainly elderly men went to seek refuge with the Dutch UNPROFOR battalion stationed at Potocari. A second group, made up of roughly 15.000 mostly unarmed, able-bodied Muslim men, was forced at Susnjari in the evening of 11 July 1995 and fled, in one enormous column, through the woods in the direction of the Tuzla, a zone controlled by the Bosnian Serb government. The evidence is that whichever option was chosen, Bosnian Muslims allegedly faced a similar fate of deportation, summary or mass execution, torture, rape, or other humiliations. Nightmarish scenes have been evoked, which would, as the Confirming Judge noted during his initial review of the indictment, "fill the darkest pages of human history." Massacres in the woods: The evidence in the case file and the testimony during the hearing establishes prima facie that in the morning of 12 July 1995, Bosnian Serb soldiers stationed along the Bratunac-Nova Kasaba road, having APCs, tanks, anti-aircraft guns and artillery, set numerous ambushes for the column of Bosnian Muslims trying to reach Tuzla through the woods. Ensnared behind Bosnian Serb lines and lured by guarantees of safety promised by the Serbs, a number of those fleeing surrendered or were taken prisoner. In either event, thousands of Muslims were summarily executed either at the very place of their vend surrender, of capture, or elsewhere. Many witnesses reported the infiltration of the column by Bosnian Serb soldiers who gave the crowd erroneous directions in order to direct people toward ambushes or toward the Bratunac-Nova Kasaba road where the army lay in wait for them. It is alleged that the barbarity of the methods of execution and mutilation used by Bosnian Serb troops was such that Muslim refugees were seized by a wave of frenzy and that many of them committed suicide. Among the methods mentioned in testimony, the survivors of massacres made special reference to dumdum bullets and knives. At the hearing, the investigator, Jean-Rene Ruez, described the horror of some of the scenes. Survivors told how a man was forced to eat the liver of his grandson, the throat of whom had been cut before his eyes by a Serbian soldier, and how a woman watched helplessly as her baby was executed by stabbing with a bayonet. The Tribunal has chose Tribunal has deliberately chosen not to describe any others here. Mass executions at Kravica: On 13 July 1995, it is alleged a large group of approximately 500 to 1.000 Bosnian Muslims, who had been surrounded after the ambush at Kamenica, surrendered to Bosnian Serb soldiers on the asphalt road there and were directed to a field at Sandici and then on foot towards Kravica. They were forced into hangar which could barely hold all its members. The soldiers surrounding the hangar opened fire through all the hangar's apertures and threw grenades inside. With a few rare exceptions, this group was exterminated. Mass executions near Karakaj Lazete: According to the descriptions by survivors, the massacres at Karakaj unfolded according to the following scenario: After their surrender or capture, thousands of the Muslims who had initially been part of the column fleeing towards Tuzla were led toward various assembly or transit points, notably a soccer field at Nova Kasaba, a hangar at Bratunac, then towards Grbavci school facility near Karakaj. During the day of 14 July 1995, Bosnian Serb soldiers took all the Muslim detainees out of the school in small groups and boarded them on trucks. Blindfolded or with their hands tied behind their backs, the detainees were subsequently driven either to a field near the school of Grbavci or to the artificial lake of a dam where they were all executed. Those showing signs of life were finished off by individual shots. Present at one of the sites, General Mladic saw the execution of the detainees who were there when he passed. An excavator, thereafter, dug a mass grave. The massacres took place from about noon to midnight on 14 July 1995, the trucks arriving at the execution areas every 10 to 15 minutes. The number of persons executed at this site was estimated at 2.500 by one of the survivors. During the same day, a witness at the Konjevici intersection saw three buses full of men, followed by a wheeled APC and an excavator, take a turnoff towards Cerska. Those buses later headed back without their occupants. Mass executions at a farm at Branjevo and other places: According to testimony at the hearing given by Drazen Erdemovic, also indicted by this Tribunal, Muslim civilians previously held in the school at Pilica were taken by bus, on 16 July 1995, to a farm at Branjevo. This group of 1.200 people was executed in its entirety by soldiers of the unit to which Drazen Erdemovic belonged. He also participated in the executions. After 16 July 1996, many groups of Muslims still trying to reach Tuzla through the woods continued to be savagely killed by Bosnian Serb soldiers: half of a group of 150 people at Konjevic Polje and another group of 150 people at Udric. On 17 July 1995, 250 people who were captured were gathered around what was to be their grave and were pushed into it alive by an excavator. Summary executions at Potocari: Potocari and its environs were the assembly point for most of the Muslim women, children, elderly and invalids who had journeyed to the UNPROFOR compound held by the Dutch Battalion. Since not all of them were able to find protection there, many spent the night of 11 to 13 July 1995 in the neighbouring factories and were then transferred by truck to the areas controlled by the Muslim government forces. The few fighting-age men present were transported toward execution sites. Potocari and its environs were the scene of summary executions. Several hundred people were allegedly selected and then cruelly massacred with knives. For several hours on 12 July 1995, Serbian soldiers randomly selected refugees among the crowd of Muslims, collected them together in small groups of ten, and led them behind the 11th of March factory where they were mutilated with knives and had their throats cut. It took a truck about five trips to collect the bodies of those thus executed. This selection and execution process allegedly continued until the morning of 13 July. These arbitrary massacres were of such exceptional cruelty and created such a degree of terror and panic amid the remaining Muslims that some of them were given to commit suicide. Horrific scenes reported by witnesses tell of several babies being killed with knives before their mothers' eyes. The International Criminal Tribunal has not been requested to review under what conditions the enclave was defended. The Prosecutor, nonetheless, requested that Colonel Karremans, Commander of the Dutch Battalion, and two of his men testify. In his testimony, the corps leader described the impetus of his unit in avoiding the tragedy even though he did recognise a list of the men present among the refugees allegedly given to a Serbian officer by one of his men. The corps leader suggested several causes. He spoke about the imbalance of men and weapons, the logistical and psychological impact on the battalion of the blockade of the enclave, an unfavourable international context. Before concluding, he said: "On 25 May, in a very long report, I informed all the hierarchical levels and my authorities that I was no longer in a position to carry out my submission and execute my orders. In fact, this signalled the end of my mission. We then began to do what we could, to improvise. By doing this, we succeeded in holding out until 6 July, which was part of our mission." The material in the confirmation file, along with the additional evidence tendered by the Prosecutor at the hearing, bears out the following conclusions: The following places in Bosnian Serb-held Bosnia and Herzegovina were used as prisoner assembly or transit points: Srebrenica, Potocari, Bratunac, Sandici, Nova Kasaba, a school at Tisca, Lazete, a school at Grbavci, a school at Pilica. The following places were execution sites: Srebrenica, Potocari, an area at the Konjevici intersection and an area all along the route between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba, the Jadar River, the Cerska Valley, the hills near Vlasenica, Lazete, the plateau at the dam of Lazete, the farm at Branjevo. Mass graves have been identified at the following places: Two at Tatar Glogova, three potential ones are near the Nova Kasaba soccer field, one in the Cerska Valley, two at the execution site at Lazete, and at the farm at Branjevo. All of these operations leading to and following the fall of the Srebrenica enclave took place under the supervision of General Ratko Mladic, to whose presence at the decisive moments there has been more than sufficient attestation. Upon entering Srebrenica, Mladic spoke to the press in those terms: "That's it. As of 11 July 1995, Srebrenica is Serb. On the eve of another great Serbian feast day, we are offering the city to the Serbian people. Finally, after the rebellion against the Dahijas, the moment has arrived for us to take vengeance on the Turks in this region." Around the UN Compound at Potocari, General Mladic was present on 12 July 1995. He was seen giving a short interview to reporters and speaking to the crowd whom he pretended to appease. On his orders, the men were separated from the women and loaded onto buses. At Bratunac on 13 July 1995, Mladic went to see the detainees in a hangar and told them that they would subsequently be exchanged. In the night of 13 to 14 July 1995, when the detainees were evacuated toward the school at Grbavci, Mladic was seen given instructions to his troops. Mladic was also present at Sandici and spoke to a large throng of prisoners held there and reiterated the same reassurances. Mass executions followed his departure. On 13 July 1995, he spoke to a crowd of prisoners before their transfer to Nova Kasaba and participated first in separating a group of some thirty men from among the prisoners. On 14 July 1995, General Mladic was at the school at Grbavci and spoke to the prisoners once again. His departure was immediately followed by the transfer of the detainees towards an execution site. It was at that site that he was subsequently seen in the evening by Witness A, one of those who survived the massacre. Specifically in respect of the events at Kravica and the Branjevo farm, which do not appear in the indictment of 16 November but whose occurrence has been abundantly demonstrated during the hearings, the Trial Chamber invites the Prosecutor to supplement the indictment. Pursuant to the scheme that we have decided to follow, we will now start the fourth part, responsibility of the alleged offences: Individual criminal responsibility. The facts presented by the Prosecutor in support of the indictment permit the inference to be drawn that the offences charged were committed in accordance with a political programme and an institutional and military organisation whose background is here summarised. The Trial Chamber will then analyse the seizure of power in several parts of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the consequences of that seizure. First, the historical and political context of the offences charged. Bosnia and Herzegovina was one of the six republics in two autonomous regions which constituted the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the SFRY. After the last convention of the league of League of Communists, the LCY, on 20 January 1990, which unanimously abrogated the dominant role of the Communist Party, elections were organised in all the republics. Parliamentary elections were held in Bosnia and Herzegovina in November and December 1990 in which three nationalist parties emerged victorious: the SDA (Party of Democratic Action) for the Muslims, the Serbian Democratic Party (SDS), and the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ). After the elections, the three parties formed a coalition and divided the main institutional positions within the republic among themselves. The president of the republic was a Bosnian Muslim, Alija Izetbegovic; the head of the parliament a Serb, Momcilo Krajisnik; and the Prime Minister, a Croat, Jure Pelivan. Despite the apparent consensus, it seems that the objective of the SDS was different from that of the other parties represented in the republic's institution, it being to seize power in certain regions of the republic. Political preparation: The programme of Serbian - The programme of the Serbian Democratic Party (SDS) of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the concept of a Greater Serbia: The Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina was founded - I will now call it the SDS - was founded in July 1990 in anticipation of the elections scheduled in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the end of the year. The themes it used can be understood only in the light of the process of dissolution of the SFRY. Its stated goal was the defence of the rights of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. During the conference which led to the founding of the party in July 1990, Radovan Karadzic, who became its president, insisted on the need to grant total equality to the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina and alleged that the Serbian nation was being destroyed by the system in place and by the so-called genocide continuously being perpetrated Defence the Serbs. To a great extent, the programme was similar to the one supported to all Serbian nationalists in the SFRY, which was given a voice in the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1986 condemning an alleged bureaucratic shift of the regime in Yugoslavia as well as, and I quote, "physical, political, legal, and cultural genocide" which would be perpetrated in Kosovo against the Serbian population in that province. The nationalist trend expressed in that text was used by the new power in Serbia. The President of the Communist League of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, at the start of 1987, launched a "anti-bureaucratic revolution" at the time that he initiated a fight against decentralisation. According to Professor Paul Guarde, the expert
